strengths: Originality/significance: TRIM presents a simple, potentially useful forward-only approach to targeted instruction-data selection, combining attention-derived token saliency with contextual token-class fingerprints.

Soundness: The main 5% comparison covers several relevant baselines under a nominally standardized pipeline, reports three-seed means and standard deviations, and shows consistent gains across three multiple-choice tasks. The GSM8K result is especially promising, improving over LESS by 8.8 percentage points at a 5% budget.

The paper includes useful initial ablations of pooling, warmup checkpoint, number of layers, and unseen-token handling. It also evaluates two coreset budgets, transfer from a 1B scorer to two larger models, and selected-data composition.

Presentation: The method, equations, pseudocode, figures, and principal experimental setup are generally clear and well organized. Dataset sizes, model families, evaluation sample sizes, LoRA settings, and most training hyperparameters are reported.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on a tiny target set and the method's inapplicability to task-agnostic pretraining selection; these honest limitations should not count against the paper.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate selection quality from the amount of training signal. Training every coreset for the same four epochs means that subsets containing longer sequences provide more training tokens; on GSM8K, TRIM's selected examples average 446 tokens versus 323 for LESS and 259 for TAGCOS. This 38–72% token-budget advantage can directly contribute to the large accuracy gain. Compute- or token-matched training is needed before attributing the improvement to superior relevance scoring.

The claimed mitigation of length bias is not established. Showing that TRIM selects longer samples demonstrates a different length preference, not that its ranking is length-agnostic or more correct. There is no controlled analysis of score versus length, and causal attention makes column saliency intrinsically position-dependent because early tokens can be attended to by more later queries.

The central mechanistic claim—that fingerprints recover task-defining structural patterns rather than lexical overlap—is unsupported. Fingerprints are indexed by exact tokenizer classes, while unseen classes are mapped using input-embedding similarity; this construction could primarily retrieve vocabulary and formatting overlap. No comparison removes attention saliency, token-class matching, or lexical information, and no qualitative retrieval or causal intervention verifies the proposed structural explanation.

The GSM8K experiment has a serious unresolved contamination and confounding risk. The supposedly non-math/general-purpose pool contains 100,000 COT examples, and TRIM selects 67.2% of its GSM8K coreset from that source. The manuscript provides no source-level description or n-gram/semantic decontamination against GSM8K train, validation, and test items. The result may reflect retrieval of math or benchmark-derived examples rather than transfer of topic-independent reasoning structure.

The reported three-seed results apparently use one fixed set of only five target examples per multiple-choice task and ten for GSM8K. Variation over fine-tuning seeds does not measure the acknowledged dominant risk: sensitivity to which target examples are sampled. Multiple independently sampled target sets, confidence intervals, and robustness to mislabeled or unrepresentative examples are necessary.

Several methodological inconsistencies impede verification. Equation 13 has only mean-max pooling, whereas Appendix B introduces an additional coverage term with eta=0.05; Algorithm 2 mentions a coverage bonus but does not implement it. The default unseen-token 'penalty' is lambda=1, which applies no down-weighting, and the meaning of the ablation labeled 'None' is unclear. The paper also alternates between scoring at the last checkpoint and language suggesting checkpoint aggregation.

Significance/efficiency: Claims of being 'orders of magnitude faster' and operating at a 'fraction' of baseline cost are supported only by simplified asymptotic accounting. No wall-clock time, GPU-hours, peak memory, throughput, or preprocessing cost is reported. Extracting attention matrices from six layers can disable optimized attention kernels and incur substantial quadratic storage, while nearest-fingerprint search for the many unseen token classes is omitted from the cost analysis. Thus the headline practical-efficiency claim is not demonstrated.

Baseline and evaluation coverage is incomplete. Budget curves include only two of the three main tasks and omit GSM8K at intermediate budgets; transfer experiments compare only against random and TRIM's own oracle rather than transferable competing selectors; and the task-dependent choice of prompt-only, response-only, or all-token scoring is not fully specified or controlled across methods. Full-data comparisons also use the same epoch count rather than a compute-matched schedule, weakening claims that TRIM surpasses full-data tuning.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. There is no code or artifact link, exact target examples and evaluation prompts are absent, filtering and formatting of the 270,679-example pool are delegated to another repository, decoding details are not enumerated, and actual resource consumption is withheld. These omissions make exact reconstruction and contamination auditing difficult.

Presentation is polished but sometimes overstates the evidence: small, often sub-point differences are described as surpassing full-data or oracle performance without significance tests, while 'model-agnostic structure,' 'structural fidelity,' and effective length-agnosticism are inferred rather than tested.

Limitations and ethics are too narrow. The manuscript discusses licenses but not potential benchmark leakage, privacy or harmful content inherited from the instruction corpora, amplification of bias from a five-example target set, or risks of selecting homogeneous data. Given that tiny-target-set bias is acknowledged, mitigation and auditing procedures are warranted.

strengths: Soundness/significance: The empirical results show genuine promise. At a 5% budget, TRIM has the best mean accuracy in Table 1 (45.37% versus 44.21% for LESS), and its GSM8K result is particularly substantial (29.52% versus 20.72% for the strongest reported coreset baseline). Results are averaged over three training seeds, and the paper also studies multiple budgets, 1B–8B models, and cross-architecture transfer.

Originality: Constructing token-class fingerprints from attention-weighted contextual representations and using them for targeted instruction-data selection is a reasonably novel combination. The forward-only formulation is practically attractive relative to per-example gradient methods.

Presentation: The central pipeline is easy to follow, with equations, pseudocode, diagrams, baseline descriptions, dataset sizes, evaluation-set sizes, and common training hyperparameters. The manuscript also clearly distinguishes selection using a warmed model from downstream training of a fresh model.

Limitations and ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges dependence on a very small, potentially biased target set and the method's limited applicability to task-agnostic pretraining selection. It identifies the public datasets and models used and briefly discusses artifact licenses. weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not establish the paper's central causal explanation that attention saliency captures task-defining structural tokens. There is no comparison against unweighted token fingerprints, random-token weights, frequency/TF-IDF weights, or an otherwise identical representation-matching method without attention. The reported gains therefore support the complete heuristic, but not the claimed mechanism.

The saliency definition has serious unresolved positional confounds under causal attention. Column scores naturally favor early tokens because they can be attended to by more later queries, while row-entropy normalization varies with the number of available causal keys. Equation (2) is undefined for a position having one non-masked key because it divides by log(1)=0. No masking, positional-control, or numerical treatment is specified, undermining both the length-bias argument and exact reproducibility.

Evaluation uncertainty is understated. Only training-seed variation is reported; the crucial sets of merely 5–10 target examples appear fixed. There is no resampling of these sets, sensitivity analysis, or comparison of different target-set compositions. Consequently, robustness to the limitation the authors themselves identify is unknown.

Several headline conclusions overreach the evidence. The claim that TRIM surpasses full-data tuning rests on small differences for SocialIQA and HellaSwag relative to the reported standard deviations; HellaSwag improves by only 0.53 points, with the full-data standard deviation being 0.7. No confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied. Likewise, observing longer selected sequences does not demonstrate that the method is length-agnostic or that those sequences are more informative.

The GSM8K result is impressive but potentially confounded by task-specific design choices. Appendix B permits prompt-only, response-only, or all-token scoring and explicitly motivates response-only scoring for GSM8K, yet the actual scope used for each experiment is not reported, nor is it clear whether baselines receive comparable task-informed treatment. This matters because selecting response-side chain-of-thought data can directly favor the COT source.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code or configuration artifact is provided, and important details are inconsistent or missing: Equation (13) omits the coverage term later introduced in Equation (15); Algorithm 2 also omits that term despite prose claiming it is included; the selected scoring scope is unspecified; target examples and prompts are not listed; and the supposed unseen-token 'penalty' defaults to 1.0. These ambiguities can materially change rankings.

The strong efficiency claim is supported only by simplified asymptotic accounting. The authors explicitly omit wall-clock time and GPU-hours, despite claiming orders-of-magnitude speedups and a fraction of the cost. The analysis does not quantify the substantial expense and memory traffic of materializing multi-head attention matrices, nearest-fingerprint lookup, preprocessing, or end-to-end selection. Empirical runtime and peak-memory comparisons are needed.

Originality/significance are somewhat narrower than presented: the approach remains a heuristic similarity ranker built from established attention and representation signals, and evaluation covers only four reasoning benchmarks from one 270k-example pool. There is no examination of generation quality, instruction following, safety, diversity, contamination, or substantially larger corpora.

The ethics discussion is largely a license checklist. Target-conditioned selection could amplify biases or unsafe patterns present in a tiny target set, an issue closely connected to the acknowledged representativeness limitation, but the paper neither analyzes this risk nor proposes auditing or mitigation procedures.

strengths: Soundness: TRIM is a coherent forward-only selection method combining attention-derived token saliency, contextual token fingerprints, and mean-max candidate scoring. The main comparison uses a common 270,679-example pool, fresh downstream fine-tuning, three seeds, and a broad set of heuristic, representation-based, training-dynamics, and gradient-based baselines.

Empirical evidence is promising: at a 5% budget, TRIM obtains the best result on all three main tasks and improves the macro-average from LESS's 44.21% to 45.37%. The GSM8K result is particularly notable: 29.52% versus 20.72% for the strongest reported competitor and 30.25% with the full corpus.

Significance: reducing selection-time backward passes could make targeted instruction-data curation substantially more practical. The experiment in which a 1B scorer selects useful data for Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B further increases the method's practical relevance.

Originality: token-class fingerprints formed from saliency-weighted contextual states are a novel and intuitive synthesis of token-level selection, attention signals, and target-aware representation matching. The method is materially different from the sample-level gradient and representation baselines.
Presentation: the paper is well organized and visually polished. The method is explained through equations, a useful overview figure, pseudocode, ablations, and explicit dataset and training tables.

Reproducibility is partially supported by reporting model versions, corpus sizes, evaluation sets and shot counts, LoRA configuration, optimizer settings, software versions, and hardware. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges sensitivity to the tiny target set and lack of direct applicability to pretraining.

No major unresolved ethical concern is apparent for the proposed selection algorithm, and the paper discusses model and software licensing. The acknowledgment that target-set bias can propagate into selected data is appropriate.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is insufficiently demonstrated. The paper repeatedly claims orders-of-magnitude speedups or a fraction of the computational cost, but reports neither wall-clock measurements, GPU-hours, peak memory, nor measured FLOPs. Table 4 only gives coarse asymptotics and omits potentially important costs such as materializing multi-layer attention maps and nearest-fingerprint lookup.

The evidence does not establish that TRIM mitigates length bias. Figure 3 merely shows that it selects longer GSM8K-directed examples than LESS and TAGCOS; this could result from selecting more examples from the COT source. A controlled length perturbation, score-length correlation, or quality-controlled comparison is needed before calling the method length-agnostic.

The explanation of GSM8K gains as transfer of abstract reasoning structure is speculative. TRIM selects 67.2% of its GSM8K coreset from the explicitly chain-of-thought-oriented COT dataset, yet the manuscript calls the pool non-math and provides no contamination, benchmark-overlap, topical-overlap, or qualitative retrieval audit. This weakens the strongest empirical result and its stated interpretation.

Several transfer conclusions are overstated. TRIM-Transfer exceeds TRIM-Oracle by only 0.69 and 0.56 macro points, with per-task differences generally comparable to the reported standard deviations. Moreover, Table 3 lacks transferred versions of strong competing selectors. It supports transferability, but not decisively model-agnostic fingerprints or superiority in the transfer setting.

Some mathematical and implementation details need correction or clarification. Equation 2 divides by log of the number of unmasked keys, which is zero for a causal-attention row with one valid key. The default unseen-token 'penalty' is lambda=1.0 despite lambda being introduced as a down-weighting factor, and the meaning of the 'None' ablation is unclear. The main scoring equation omits the coverage term later introduced in the appendix.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no code or artifact is identified; the exact five or ten target examples, random seeds, prompt templates, decoding parameters, task-specific scoring scopes, preprocessing/filtering rules, and baseline implementation details are not fully supplied. These choices can matter substantially when selection is guided by only five examples.

Statistical support is limited to three seeds without confidence intervals or significance tests. In particular, the claimed improvements over full-data fine-tuning on SocialIQA and HellaSwag are small relative to full-data variability, so the statement that TRIM surpasses full-data training should be qualified as a comparison of point estimates.

The ablations are confined to CommonsenseQA and do not isolate the proposed attention saliency against simpler alternatives such as unweighted token fingerprints, hidden-state-only scoring, lexical token matching, or randomized saliency. Consequently, it is unclear how much of the gain comes specifically from attention-derived saliency rather than target-conditioned token matching or source-dataset routing.

The limitations and ethics treatment could be broader. The paper does not discuss privacy or harmful-content risks inherited from OASST1 and other web-derived instruction sources, nor how selection may amplify demographic or topical biases in the tiny target set. License discussion alone is not a complete data-ethics assessment.

strengths: The paper proposes a reasonably original and practically relevant combination of attention-derived token saliency, contextual token-class fingerprints, and forward-only coreset scoring. The method is clearly motivated and substantially cheaper than per-example gradient selection.

The evaluation is broad: multiple coreset budgets, four principal downstream tasks, three main target architectures, an additional Llama-3 suite, an in-domain setting, and three-seed reporting. The GSM8K result is particularly promising: at a 5% budget, TRIM obtains 29.52% versus LESS's 20.72%, close to full-data fine-tuning at 30.25%.

Measured efficiency is useful and significant: under the reported common H200 setup, selection takes 4.40 hours for TRIM versus 14.16 for TAGCOS and 35.76 for LESS. Cross-model transfer results further improve the method's practical value.
The paper is generally well organized and visually clear, and includes useful sensitivity studies for target-set size, target noise, pooling, layers, fallback penalties, and checkpoints.

The impact statement appropriately discusses compute benefits as well as bias amplification, harmful-content retention, privacy, and misuse. It recommends dataset auditing and does not claim that TRIM itself solves these issues.
weaknesses: A mathematical inconsistency undermines soundness and reproducibility. The stated IDF modification replaces every occurrence weight for token class t by alpha(v,i)*IDF(t) in Eq. 9. Because the same positive scalar multiplies every term for that class and the resulting sum is L2-normalized, IDF(t) cancels exactly and cannot alter the fingerprint. For IDF(t)=0, the fingerprint is undefined. The reported IDF ablation therefore cannot correspond to the written method without an unreported implementation difference.

The central causal claim—that attention-derived token saliency drives the gains—is not adequately isolated. There is no ablation replacing saliency weights with uniform weights, removing row or column saliency, or comparing against token-level contextual matching without attention. In contrast, the NFF ablation drops MMLU from 49.43 to 44.79, indicating that nearest-fingerprint fallback is essential. Thus, the evidence does not establish that attention saliency, rather than contextual hidden-state similarity and fallback mapping, is the decisive contribution.

Several specifications conflict. Section 3 presents IDF as part of the method, whereas Appendix H says the default uses no IDF. Eq. 13 and Algorithm 2 omit the coverage term, while Appendix C says the default score includes 0.05*coverage. Selective scoring over prompts, responses, or all tokens is described as an important hyperparameter, but the per-task choices are not clearly reported. These differences materially impede reproduction; no code or exact target-example identifiers are provided.

Eq. 2 is undefined at a causal position having one admissible key because its denominator is log(1)=0. The manuscript does not state how this case is handled. More broadly, raw attention entropy and received attention are treated as token importance without causal validation, despite known limitations of attention as explanation.

The strongest main-table advantage over LESS is small: 48.56 versus 48.27 macro-average, with per-task gaps of only 0.10, 0.28, and 0.49 points and three-seed standard deviations. No paired significance testing or uncertainty for differences is supplied, so claims of consistently outperforming state of the art are overstated. The large GSM8K gain is convincing but does not generalize uniformly across the principal tasks.

The claimed mitigation of length bias is supported only by observing that TRIM selects longer examples. Selecting a higher mean length does not itself demonstrate absence of length bias or improved causal use of long-range content. Controlled length perturbations, score-length correlations, and matched-content comparisons are needed.

Potential train-test contamination is insufficiently addressed. The candidate pool includes FLAN V2 and a 100k chain-of-thought collection, which may contain tasks or examples related to BBH, GSM8K, and other evaluations. Target-guided retrieval can preferentially select near-duplicates, yet no benchmark-level provenance or deduplication audit is reported. This is especially important for interpreting the unusually large GSM8K improvement and the characterization of the pool as non-math.

Overall, the idea and empirical signal merit further study, but the algebraic error, method-description inconsistencies, missing component ablations, and contamination uncertainty prevent others from reliably attributing or reproducing the central claims in the current form. These issues outweigh the promising efficiency and task-specific results.

strengths: The forward-only combination of attention-derived token weighting, contextual token-class fingerprints, and nearest-fingerprint fallback is a potentially useful and reasonably original approach to targeted instruction-data selection.

The evaluation is broad: multiple coreset budgets, several benchmarks, three model architectures, three-seed results, target-set sensitivity, transfer experiments, and measured wall-clock costs. The GSM8K result is especially promising (29.52% versus LESS at 20.72% for a 5% coreset), and the reported 4.40-hour selection runtime is substantially below the compared methods.
The main pipeline is presented clearly through equations, figures, and pseudocode, and the paper provides extensive supplementary experiments.
The impact statement appropriately discusses bias amplification, harmful or private data, dataset governance, and the absence of privacy or safety guarantees.
weaknesses: There is a concrete mathematical inconsistency in the IDF mechanism. For each fixed token class t, replacing every occurrence weight in Eq. (9) by alpha times IDF(t) multiplies the entire pre-normalized fingerprint by one positive scalar, which cancels under L2 normalization. IDF therefore cannot change any fingerprint or selected coreset as defined, yet Table 11 reports different performance. This indicates that either the equations, implementation, or experiment description is incorrect.

The implemented method is not reproducibly specified. Eq. (13) and Algorithm 2 omit the coverage term used by the stated default configuration; Appendix B says scoring uses a coverage bonus while its pseudocode does not; the main MMLU result is 49.33 whereas several nominally default appendix configurations report 49.43; and the prompt-only/response-only/all-token scoring scope is described as an important task-dependent hyperparameter without documenting which scope was used for each reported experiment. The discussion also alternates between last-checkpoint and multi-checkpoint aggregation.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed central contribution. There is no comparison against uniform token weights, row-only or column-only saliency, token-class matching without attention, or a token-level lexical/contextual-representation baseline. Consequently, the results cannot establish that attention-derived saliency, rather than token identity, contextual embeddings, NFF, pooling, or source-composition shifts, causes the gains. Raw causal attention also has strong positional effects—particularly for column scores—but these are neither controlled nor analyzed.

Several claims overstate the evidence. On the three main tasks, TRIM's 48.56 average is below full-data tuning at 48.99 and only 0.29 above LESS, with overlapping seed variability and no significance testing. Selecting longer examples in Figure 3 does not by itself demonstrate mitigation of length bias; it could simply reflect different source mixtures. Likewise, cross-model transfer is compared primarily with random and TRIM-oracle subsets rather than strong competing selectors.

The strongest GSM8K interpretation is vulnerable to contamination and source confounding. The supposedly general-purpose pool includes 100,000 chain-of-thought examples plus FLAN V2, but the paper provides no benchmark-overlap audit, deduplication procedure, or analysis excluding math-like/COT sources. Thus the claim that TRIM discovers latent reasoning structure in a non-math corpus is not adequately supported.

The framing around limited target supervision is misleading: MMLU uses 285 target examples rather than the repeatedly advertised 5–10, and the setting called selection “without target examples” constructs a 260-example, source-stratified reference set. Runtime comparisons are also insufficiently documented for S2L's intended small-proxy setup, and total cost—including warmup, selection, and final fine-tuning—is not compared with full-data training. Code, exact reference examples, and complete scoring configurations are unavailable, further limiting reproducibility. strengths: TRIM offers a useful and reasonably original combination of token-class fingerprints, contextual hidden-state matching, and attention-derived weighting. Its forward-only candidate scoring is practically attractive compared with per-example gradient methods.

The evaluation is broad: multiple coreset budgets, three main general benchmarks, a low-overlap GSM8K setting, cross-model transfer, in-domain math selection, target-set sensitivity, noise robustness, and supplementary model/task results. Most results use three seeds with standard deviations.

The strongest evidence is on GSM8K: at a 5% budget, TRIM obtains 29.52% versus 20.72% for LESS and nearly matches 30.25% full-data fine-tuning. The measured selection runtime of 4.40 hours versus 14.16–87.95 hours for compared methods also supports the efficiency claim under the reported setup.

Cross-model results are promising: a coreset selected by LLaMA-2-7B transfers effectively to LLaMA-2-13B and Mistral-7B, sometimes outperforming both full-data fine-tuning and in-model TRIM selection.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with an informative overview figure, explicit equations, pseudocode, dataset statistics, training hyperparameters, and extensive appendices.

The impact statement appropriately discusses compute benefits as well as risks from amplifying bias, sensitive content, and narrow target behaviors. It recommends relevant auditing and governance practices without claiming that TRIM itself solves these concerns.
weaknesses: The central claim that attention-derived saliency is responsible for TRIM's gains is not adequately isolated. The ablations vary layer count, pooling, IDF, fallback penalty, and checkpoints, but do not compare against uniform token weights or otherwise remove row/column attention saliency. Since saliency is the headline contribution, this missing ablation materially weakens the causal evidence.

The stated IDF reweighting is mathematically ineffective. Equation 9 constructs a separate fingerprint for each token class t; multiplying every occurrence weight in that fingerprint by the same IDF(t) cancels exactly between numerator and denominator. The reported IDF ablation therefore cannot reflect the described operation, indicating either an error in the specification or a mismatch with the implementation.

The method is not fully specified consistently. Equation 13 and Algorithm 2 use mean-max pooling, whereas Appendix C and the reported default add a coverage term. Selective scoring may use prompt-only, response-only, or all tokens, but the manuscript does not clearly state the scope used for each reported task. Configurations beyond MMLU are also insufficiently enumerated.

Equation 2 is undefined for a causal sequence's first token because the number of admissible keys is one and the denominator is log(1)=0. No special handling is specified. More broadly, the claimed mitigation of length bias is supported only by showing that TRIM selects longer examples; this does not establish reduced bias, and max pooling can itself increase scores with sequence length through an extreme-value effect.

On the main three-task comparison, TRIM's average improvement over LESS is only 0.29 points, with per-task differences comparable to reported seed variability and no paired tests or confidence intervals. The large gain is concentrated in GSM8K, so statements that TRIM consistently outperforms state of the art by up to 9% should distinguish percentage points from relative percent and acknowledge the limited breadth of the large effect.

Comparisons to full-data fine-tuning use a fixed number of epochs, so the full-data model receives far more optimization steps and may suffer from mixture interference or a mismatched training budget. Consequently, occasional superiority over full-data training is not by itself strong evidence that the selected subset is intrinsically better.

The runtime comparison assumes a common 7B scoring model and implementation, although methods such as S2L are designed around small proxy models. FLOPs, peak memory, sequence-length/token throughput, preprocessing, and implementation optimization are not reported, limiting the generality and fairness of the efficiency conclusion.

No code or runnable artifact is identified. Together with the specification inconsistencies, missing task-specific settings, and reliance on processed data from another repository, this prevents reliable reproduction despite the otherwise useful training details.

The originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the work combines established attention-saliency, prototype matching, and coreset-ranking ideas. Stronger mechanistic ablations are needed to show that the attention-weighted token construction contributes beyond a simpler contextual token-prototype retrieval baseline.
